title: What this means for energy traders — Wednesday, November 4, 2026

sections.overall: Geopolitics dominates today's flow. Crude fell on hopes of diplomacy over the Iran war, and the political backdrop shifted after the US midterms. Beneath that, the long-term LNG contracting story continues, with Gulf and Asian buyers locking in supply from US and Australian projects. Every tracked trend is rated STEADY: companies keep acting on them, but none is accelerating or fading this week.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Crude has moved lower across several sessions. CNBC reports prices below $90 a barrel on Wednesday after Vice President Vance tied Republican midterm losses to the Iran war (CNBC). On Monday Brent was at $105.55, its lowest in more than two weeks (The Guardian). Markets usually treat credible diplomacy as lowering the supply-risk premium, and reversals in talks tend to bring it back. Supply is still constrained: global refinery inputs fell 4.8 million b/d in 2Q26 (EIA). It remains unclear whether the diplomatic signals become a concrete deal.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: The clearest corporate signal is long-term LNG contracting. QatarEnergy's 20-year order from Woodside's Louisiana project follows its earlier US deals in the ledger, and the FT reports Qatar is set to become the biggest buyer of US LNG (FT). In Asia, TotalEnergies' heads of agreement with Jiangsu Guoxin and XRG's purchase of Shell's Australian stake show the same demand for secured supply. In Europe, Germany missed its winter storage target, which leaves it more exposed to spot purchases (FT). Preliminary agreements are not binding, so conversion to final contracts is a point to track.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: Refining margins are still tied to the Iran and Ukraine conflicts. Nine large oil firms are on track for more than $95bn in profit two quarters in a row (The Guardian). Ukraine has resumed refinery strikes, and New Jersey's governor is opposing Russian diesel cargoes. These items show how policy and supply disruption feed into diesel availability.
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: Policy and integrity news led. Verra received its first ICVCM approval for transition credits from early coal retirement, and Gabon agreed a sale of about 6 million sovereign forest credits to a German state-owned energy company (Carbon Pulse). EU lawmakers backed a higher MSR threshold (Carbon Pulse), and Carbon Pulse reports EUAs recovered some losses as funds raised net length (Carbon Pulse). Verra is also responding to a watchdog report on audits. Buyer-side removal demand is described by Senken as far below what net-zero targets would imply.
